extractedText: Korea's 88 Trillion Won Population Budget Split Across 24 Agencies■ Paper Presented to Korean Association of Public Finance Proposes Pre-Review System 88 Trillion Won Budget Spread Over 24 Agencies, Coordination Needed Pre-Review Would Cut Overlap and Reset PrioritiesFinance|Published 2026.08.30. 10:43:43|By Kim Hye-rankhr@sedaily.com|Summary|SaveAAAA children's goods store at a department store in Seoul. Yonhap NewsSouth Korea's 88 trillion won ($64 billion) population policy budget, set up to address low birth rates and population aging, is being spent across 24 government agencies with too little coordination to meet its policy goals, researchers said. Population issues extend beyond childbirth and child-rearing into welfare, employment and education, they said, making a ministry-by-ministry approach insufficient.The proposal came in a paper titled "The Need for and Approaches to Introducing a Pre-Review System for Population Policy Budgets," released recently by Kim Pyung-sik, an economics professor at Kyung Hee University; Lee Jung-in, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute of Public Finance; and Kim Young-jik, a doctoral candidate at Sungkyunkwan University's Graduate School of Governance, according to public finance academics on the 30th.The researchers analyzed central government spending under the 2025 implementation plan for low birth rates and an aging society to examine how population policy money is dispersed among ministries and where coordination is needed. The budget under review totaled about 88.3 trillion won, or 13% of total government spending.Population policy currently runs through 283 programs divided among 24 administrative agencies. With multiple ministries splitting budgets and programs, the link between policy goals and individual programs can weaken, the researchers said. Low birth rate programs showed a pronounced pattern of multi-ministry collaboration, while some aging-related areas were run largely by a single ministry.It is difficult to assess how much each ministry's programs contribute to the overall goals of population policy, the researchers said, arguing for a coordination framework built around those goals. They proposed a "pre-review system for population policy budgets," under which a lead agency would examine programs for overlap and set priorities before ministries submit their budget requests.Separate budget coordination frameworks already exist for national research and development, disaster safety and official development assistance, the researchers noted, but no such function covers the population policy budget, which is larger than any of them.To run the system, the researchers proposed expert working groups in six areas: pregnancy, childbirth and child-rearing; young adults and housing; family-friendly policy; welfare for older adults; responses to a shrinking society; and expanding the economically active population. They also proposed a tiered review, applying a simplified process to recurring programs while strengthening expert scrutiny of new and strategic ones.They stressed that review findings should carry legal authority so they feed into actual budget decisions, with exemptions kept narrow to keep the system effective."Population policy involves many ministries and the budget is large, so it takes considerable time to grasp the structure of these programs," the researchers said. "A dedicated support body is needed that can compile and analyze data on an ongoing basis."#PopulationPolicy#KoreaBudget#LowBirthRate#PopulationAging#FiscalPolicy#BudgetReformOriginal reporting by Kim Hye-ran for Seoul Economic Daily.AI-translated from Korean.
